title: A Moment of Perfection

paragraphs.text: In the 1950s, cattle breeders worked with the artist Ralph Knowles to create a model profile for Guernsey cattle. Together they produced an image which has been the benchmark, the standard against which all Guernsey cattle are measured, for generations of American cattle breeders, and continues to be the representation of perfection for exacting farmers today.

Knowles grew up in the US town of Greene, Maine, on a small farm. He’d always loved art as a young man, but it wasn’t until his 30s that he became an artist. Flicking through the Guernsey Breeders Journal one day, he learnt that the American Guernsey Association (AGA) was seeking to modernise its ‘ideal’ cow. The AGA had a tradition of representing the ideal animal in a portrait of what the ‘alpha cow’ might look like. By 1959, the previous Guernsey model, painted in 1929, was outdated, and the AGA wanted a new and improved model.

‘They wanted a bigger cow,’ Knowles later recalled in an interview with his local paper. ‘Something that could eat more... and produce more milk.’ At that time Knowles’ own farm was struggling and he needed extra cash. So he wrote to the AGA to say he’d paint the beautiful cow.

Ralph Knowles, however, had no formal art training. He had received his first oil set at age 13 from his grandparents, and was largely self-taught. Over the years he’d made several cow paintings for Maine and Massachusetts dairymen, but the ideal required work of a superior level. So the farmer painted what he knew and, amazingly, the AGA took up his offer.
They soon started mailing him bundles of cow photos, noting what they admired most about each beast. ‘We like this good head on a cow, and these good feet, so forth and so on,’ Knowles recalled.

To understand what Knowles was taking on it is necessary to know some of the history of the breed. The real birthplace of Guernsey cattle is the Isle of Guernsey, a small island in the English Channel off the coast of France. When monks arrived there in 960 AD, they brought with them the best bloodlines of French cattle: Norman Brindles, also known as Alderneys, from the province of Isigny, and the famous Froment du Leon breed from Brittany, in France. Over a millennium the Guernsey breed developed from these two types of cattle. Although much later, their actual date of introduction to America is highly disputed. It was this breed which Knowles was guaranteeing to perfect.

As he studied the photographs and he submitted sketches, the ‘ideal’ Guernsey began to emerge. The cow was large, with tight shoulders, a full udder, flat rump and a long head. The AGA still keeps copies of letters from dairymen across the US with suggestions for the artist painting their perfect beast. These tell the story of how the image that Knowles created existed in the minds of farmers and breeders across the country.

‘Needless to say I like it very much... However, the head, nose and mouth seem too narrow and weak,’ wrote Dean H H Kildee of Iowa State College after reviewing the original pencil sketch. ‘I am confident that Mr Knowles will have more strength at the floor of the chest,’ he added. ‘The head doesn’t have quite the right shape... the tail bone was a little too refined and lacked the thickness near the top which you normally find,’ contributed Eugene C Meyer, a dairyman at Fort Atkinson, Wisconsin. ‘The switch* is a little too pronounced and actually reaches the ground... I believe you will see that the rear udder shows more fullness.’

To Knowles, everyone was a critic, but constructively so. Even Meyer concluded his letter with a positive prediction. ‘The finished product will stand for more years than you and I will be around; we felt it was important enough to make any suggestions that might improve it.’

After nine months of fine-tuning, Knowles felt the portrait was finished. The AGA flew the artist and his painting from Maine to Toronto, where the group’s annual meeting was held. That night, his first ever in a hotel, Knowles was called upon one more time to make an adjustment to the painting. The committee had decided to ‘dehorn’ its ideal cow: the first dairy breed to do so. The ever-patient Knowles obliged by painting out the horns; an adjustment that can be seen on the original painting today.

The next day must have been a relief for the young farmer. While he ended up living a long and happy life — becoming a Guernsey breeder of renown — he probably never again reached the heights of that moment when the curtain was raised and his painting revealed. However, today his painting continues to epitomise an ideal Guernsey, and his moment of perfection is still on display for all to see.
